extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political science studying American party machines and electoral practice
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate how party nominating machinery (primaries, committees, conventions) operates and the criteria by which its results should be judged (freedom of choice, fitness of office-holders, procedural fairness). The chapter describes practical mechanisms, abuses, and contextual factors that affect the quality of nominations and elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of choice (representativeness of nomination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the choice of candidates for office really free — i.e. does it represent the unbiassed wish and mind of the voters generally?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly presented as one of 'the tests by which one may try the results of the system.' Used to judge whether the nomination process genuinely reflects voter preferences rather than being dictated by party managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of office-holders (probity and capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the offices filled by men of probity and capacity sufficient for the duties?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named alongside 'freedom of choice' as the second principal test of the nominating system's results. Evaluates whether nominees are honest and capable for the public offices they will occupy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prearrangement of meetings and nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings should be prearranged: select chairman and speakers, have resolutions ready, and prepare lists of candidates or delegates beforehand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as practically indispensable to make public meetings 'go off well'; the author notes this 'practically curtail[s] the freedom of the meeting' but argues the alternative is confusion. Guidance includes preparing for adverse resolutions/hostile amendments and having lists settled in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/complexity of offices and elections as a quality factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The great number of offices and frequency of elections increases the work of the machine and reduces ordinary citizens' ability to form informed judgments about many candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: long ballot papers with many columns (Chicago 1908: 195 candidates), many annual and multi-year conventions; conclusion that abundant offices make it hard to find adequate delegates and increase reliance on party guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for expert management of statutory primaries
rubrics_metrics.description: New statutory (direct) primaries are so complex that experts familiar with primary and election law are required to organize and run them properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: 'The direct nomination device ... render it necessary to have abler experts who understand not only the mysteries of the regular election law but the added mysteries of the primary law as well.' Failure to have expertise makes manipulation easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and composition of the primary roll ('check list')
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of a primary is determined by the roll or 'check list' of ward voters prepared by the managing committee, who try to include only men they can trust or control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include restrictive admission rules, requiring pledges to obey the committee, rejecting applicants on pretexts (e.g., recent failure to vote), and keeping bogus names on the roll. Used as a central means for managers to secure a subservient primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of membership pledges and exclusion of independents
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary membership often requires a pledge to support the party nominees, and those who refuse are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites enrollment/pledge practices (New York 1899 law example) and notes independent-minded men are often excluded, producing a compliant primary electorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packing, padding, and bogus rolls as evidence of manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping names of former members who left or died, adding outsiders, and maintaining 'voting stock' for later use — tactics that render rolls largely bogus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author provides concrete allegations and historical attendance statistics (e.g., very low percentage turnout in primaries) to illustrate how these practices enable committee control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee control of delegate selection and secret prearrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Local party committees convene primaries/conventions with predetermined lists of delegates and settle names in secret, presenting a 'cut and dry' list to assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how committees propose chairs, bring forward their list of delegates, and, if necessary, modify lists to 'preserve the unity of the party.' If the meeting contains professionals, lists are accepted without debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman and rulesmanship as instruments of control
rubrics_metrics.description: The chairman (temporary and permanent) can influence outcomes by naming the credentials committee, ruling on points of order, adjourning meetings, and other procedural maneuvers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include a partisan chairman being 'a solid 8 to 7 man all the time,' declaring lists carried during disturbances, and using procedural power to exclude opponents or decide close questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credentials/contested-seats committee usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A committee on credentials examines delegates' titles and can exclude suspected opponents on technical grounds, thereby shaping the convention's composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary chairman usually names a credentials committee favorable to professionals; exclusion of rival delegates is a common outcome unless claims are indisputably valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intimidation, fraud, and roughs in contests
rubrics_metrics.description: When needed, professionals may bring in outsiders ('roughs'), provoke disturbances, or employ fraud (e.g., 'pudding ballots') to secure desired outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and citations: Baltimore 'pudding ballots' and witness testimony describing routine cheating in primaries; violence and fraud are more likely at nominating meetings than at general elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination by acclamation as indicator of prearrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a convention has been properly packed the candidate proposed by professionals is 'nominated by acclamation,' reflecting prearranged results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rivals exist a vote may be necessary, but acclamation usually signals that the managers' predetermined choice has prevailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage nature of campaigns: nomination then election
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections have two stages — first to nominate the candidates you desire, then to carry them at the polls — and often the nomination stage (primaries) is the more decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that 'everything turns upon' securing the primaries and that in many districts nomination by the dominant party equates to election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification meetings' symbolic role
rubrics_metrics.description: Public 'ratification' gatherings after conventions are largely symbolic and attended only by those prepared to support the nominations; they have no practical importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as ceremonies where candidates are 'solemnly adopted' by the crowd but not forums for genuine deliberation or decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual vulnerability factors for machine capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain contextual conditions increase susceptibility to party-machine perversion: a vast population of ignorant immigrants; leading men intensely occupied with business; and communities so large that people know little of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explains how these conditions (especially in large U.S. cities) facilitate enrollment/manipulation of new voters, reduce civic engagement, and make political work the preserve of professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low primary turnout as evidence of professional control
rubrics_metrics.description: Very low attendance at primaries (small percentages of party voters participating) indicates management by party professionals rather than broad popular involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical attendance figures are cited (e.g., some districts with 2–10% participation; examples of primaries electing delegates by very few voters) to show how small, managed assemblies choose delegates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional politicians' objectives (patronage and office capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals aim to seize local offices and command local party votes to extract shares of State and Federal offices, legislation, and patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the motive structure behind manipulative behavior: control of local machinery translates into jobs, commissions, and opportunities for graft — explaining why the temptation to pervert machinery is strong in big cities.
